title_en: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says
title_fa: Meta’s AI agent Muse is mixing up conversations and could be exposing private data, report says
excerpt_en: In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn't belong to them.
excerpt_fa: In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn't belong to them.
content_en:
Meta employees have raised concerns that the company’s AI agent Muse has been mixing up conversations across different accounts and exposing private user data, according to a new Reuters report that looked at internal company posts.
In some of these instances, employees said Muse surfaced messages about childcare requests they never made, career advice they never asked for, product orders they never placed, and bank account balances that didn’t belong to them.
One employee told colleagues that Muse had randomly sent an extra message in a chat about weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”
In another example, an employee using the AI agent on her personal phone received a reminder from Muse to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, the popular end-to-end encrypted messaging app.
“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post, according to the report.
“Employee testing is core to the product development process and the entire point is to get feedback, so we can implement safety and privacy protections and improve products,” a Meta spokesperson said in an email to TechCrunch. “Importantly, employees have access to different versions of Muse than the public, so they’re often reviewing features, functionality, and behavior not available elsewhere.”
Launched in September, Muse is one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads.
Update 11/19/2026 12:05 PM PT: The article was updated to include Meta’s comment.

title_en: Apple HomePod mini 2 review: A necessary, but underwhelming update
title_fa: Apple HomePod mini 2 review: A necessary, but underwhelming update
excerpt_en: The most notable upgrade on the HomePod mini 2 is its S10 chip, which is supposed to power Siri AI, but that's still in the works.
excerpt_fa: The most notable upgrade on the HomePod mini 2 is its S10 chip, which is supposed to power Siri AI, but that's still in the works.
content_en:
Apple HomePod mini 2 review: A necessary, but underwhelming update
Siri AI? More like Siri MIA.
I'd be willing to forgive you if you forgot about the new HomePod mini. The overhauled smart speaker played a supporting role at best during Apple's Welcome Home event last month, behind the HomeView, and probably, in some minds, behind the updated Apple TV 4K. Still, the company provides a few upgrades in the HomePod mini 2 ($149), ensuring that it's ready for Siri AI and the assistant's newfound ability to offer personalized context for your queries. The main problem? The speaker doesn't yet support the recently upgraded virtual assistant Apple spent years improving.
What's new on the HomePod mini 2?
The most notable update on the HomePod mini 2 is on the inside. Apple swapped in its S10 chip from the Apple Watch Series 10, kicking the nearly antique S5 silicon to the curb. For a Watch comparison, that's like going from a Series 5 or first-gen Watch SE, which debuted in 2019 and 2020 respectively, to the 2024 edition. It's a big leap, and it's one Apple says was necessary for the HomePod mini to work with Siri AI.
The recently updated assistant isn't all the S10 is helping with here. Apple says the component can run real-time music evaluation "to optimize dynamic range, loudness and acoustic performance," with a hand from "advanced computational analysis." When connected to the newly introduced fourth-gen Apple TV 4K, you can use four HomePod mini 2 speakers as a surround sound setup. That S10 chip helps the speakers recognize their positions in a room and adjust the lag, convey that info to Apple's streaming box, and audio levels accordingly.
I only have two HomePod mini 2s, so I wasn't able to test this configuration, but I did hear it during Apple's event in October. Even with that brief experience, I can tell you using two second-gen HomePods as the front speakers and two HomePod minis as the rears is a much better setup. The HomePod mini doesn't muster enough bass to be a great home theater speaker on its own, and those full-size HomePods bring the boom when an action scene demands it.
Before now, you could send audio from a Mac to a HomePod mini, but Apple has expanded the functionality so that the second-gen model can serve as persistent default speakers. This means, in theory, they'll stay connected to your Mac as the primary output rather than just relying on a temporary AirPlay link. This allows you to use the HomePod mini 2, or a pair of them, for everything on your computer — from FaceTime calls to games — without having to think about connecting each app or session to the speaker(s).
The HomePod line has always had lights on the top, but they haven't really done much. Before now, the top touch panel would light up if audio was playing or display an animation when you chatted with Siri. With a new feature called Sound Glow, those lights now show hues that compliment a song's album artwork. The lights move in real time, reacting to the bass and treble in each tune. If you opt for a soundscape, Sound Glow reacts to that too, showing an animation that resembles the pitter patter of rain drops, for example. It isn't a game-changing feature, but it's a nice use of lighting that was barely utilized previously.
Lastly, there are the new colors. The HomePod mini 2 comes in pink, green, blue, white and midnight (dark grey), with those first three coordinating well with Apple's iMac colors. That list means the company retired orange and yellow from the previous generation, both of which looked great in their time. As you can see, my review units are green, and I've enjoyed the pop of color they've added to my desk over the last few weeks.
Sound quality and speed remain the same
Given that Apple saw fit to bestow a "2" on this HomePod mini, I expected some upgrades to overall sound quality to be in the mix. Unfortunately, I can't notice a difference between old and new models. Sometimes I think there's some variation, but it's not substantial enough that I'm sure, and it's not consistent across various musical styles. I do like the audio performance of the HomePod mini for its size, but it still has a sound profile of crisp highs and prominent mids offset by bass tone that lacks dynamics and depth. It's good enough for casual listening or background tunes, but not for anything more than that.
Despite the lack of Siri AI, I was hoping the S10 chip would provide a performance boost for the old Siri experience you have to settle for right now. However, the assistant's responses to basic questions took the same amount of time as they do on the first-gen model. To be clear, they're quick on both devices, I'm merely pointing out there's no difference in this regard. Just don't try to ask the old assistant to dive into Apple's core apps for you, or try to have an on-going conversation — neither request will bear any fruit.
What's not so good about the HomePod mini 2?
The biggest issue with the HomePod mini 2 right now is its biggest omission: Siri AI. The recently updated assistant isn't available on the speaker yet, and Apple hasn't provided a timeline for its arrival either. The upgraded HomePod mini is equipped to support the now-current-gen Siri, thanks to the S10 chip. However, you'll have to wait for Siri's newfound contextual awareness to dive into your Messages, Calendar and other apps on your iPhone or iPad. And to me, that's a huge miss for Apple on an overhauled smart speaker. You'll also have to wait for the more conversational chats with Siri as the HomePod mini 2 doesn't yet support those either.
I like the idea of using a HomePod mini 2 or a stereo pair of them as a persistent computer speaker with a Mac, but it's not a great experience in practice. Any time you do anything — start a song, pause a song, skip tracks — there's a 1-2 second delay in the audio responding. The lights on the top of the speakers, including the Sound Glow effect, will stop shining immediately, but the...

title_en: You won't find this fan favorite feature in GTA 6
title_fa: You won't find this fan favorite feature in GTA 6
excerpt_en: Replaying missions is possible, but not easy.
excerpt_fa: Replaying missions is possible, but not easy.
content_en:
You won't find this fan favorite feature in GTA 6
Replaying missions is possible, but not easy.
Some of the more hardcore fans, running on little-to-no sleep, might be working their way through the missions in the Grand Theft Auto 6. Unlike in its predecessor though, GTA 6 has no option to replay completed story missions. That marks a major change from the previous game, which allowed players to run back finished mission from the pause menu, mostly to retry its skill challenges. (Those haven't reappeared, either.)
Even after more than 100 hours playing the game for his review, GamesRadar editor-in-chief Josh West said that he found no replay option. Other early-access reviewers are reporting the same. So, the only way back into a mission, at least for now, is to load a manual save made before it started, and before autosave overwrites itself.
Mission replay and gold medals in GTA 5
Mission replay was first added to The Ballad of Gay Tony, the second Grand Theft Auto 4 expansion, back in 2009. It also introduced a scoring system that graded players on secondary mission goals like completion time, damage taken and headshots. Replay was introduced essentially so players could go back and get a better score. Then, with GTA 5, those goals became bronze, silver and gold medals, and achievements tied to attaining them. Rockstar's Red Dead Redemption 2's also had a "Gold Rush" trophy, which also asked for 70 gold medals out of the 104 available via its story missions.
GTA 6 has no gold medal objectives at all, at least as things stand now. Instead, challenges can be found in their own section of the progress menu. They cover broader goals rather than being mission-specific, and mostly unlock cheats once the story is completed. Rockstar North's co-studio head Rob Nelson told IGN that Rockstar had made "a very conscious effort to open things up where possible" in GTA 6's missions. Players will now find that some missions suggest an optimal route that players can ignore, for example, with the job turning into a police chase rather than ending in failure.
Red Dead Redemption 2 players long complained that straying from set paths could fail missions. That, along with GTA 5's mission medals enforcing a linear playstyle, seems to be the reason why Rockstar left them out.
How to revisit a GTA 6 mission
GTA 6 gives us 15 save slots. That might seem generous on the face of it, but it's not all that many for a campaign that has more than 90 main missions. Sharper minds than I have worked out that keeping a route back to everything would mean a fresh manual save roughly every 6.6 percent of the way through the game.
The missing mission repeat feature probably comes down to how sprawling GTA 6's story is. Entire missions can play out differently based on decisions players made earlier, sometimes without knowing they were making them. A heist, for example, can be buttery smooth or turn into an awful mess depending on gameplay completed hours earlier. Story choices also shape the wider world, down to which characters live and die. Reloading a mission and playing it in isolation would ignore the choices that set it up originally.
It's not all bad news: Races, stunts, pool and other minigames are repeatable, as are shop robberies and the bank jobs as the story unlocks. Robbed locations gray out on the map and reset after a cooldown.
And obviously GTA 6's story was designed to support repeat playthroughs, but that's a big commitment. Nelson himself — the game's lead dev — has said his playthrough took 80 hours, covering the main story and some optional goals. In GTA 5, you could jump back into a favorite mission in a few minutes, but now, playing one differently means planning saves in advance or committing to another full run. Whether that changes remains to be seen.

title_en: How to switch camera views in GTA 6
title_fa: How to switch camera views in GTA 6
excerpt_en: The game only offers a first-person perspective in very limited circumstances.
excerpt_fa: The game only offers a first-person perspective in very limited circumstances.
content_en:
How to switch camera views in GTA 6
The game only offers a first-person perspective in very limited circumstances.
Grand Theft Auto 6 gives players lots of ways to customize the experience, from the clothes the protagonists wear to granular user interface controls. Being able to shift your perspective of the action is part of that. Rockstar has long offered GTA players the ability to reposition the camera, and you can do that this time around as well.
In the camera tab of the settings menu, you can adjust the height of the camera while you're on foot, as well as the horizontal and vertical follow speeds. You have similar options for land and water vehicles, along with specific follow speeds based on whether you're the driver or a passenger. When it comes to aircraft, you can adjust the follow speed and determine whether the camera follows your plane when you do a barrel roll.
When you're out there exploring the map in a land or water vehicle, you can change the height of the camera on the fly. To switch between the three options, hold the down button on the D-pad, pick the height you want and confirm. You'll also be able to switch to the cinematic camera mode here. This makes things like high-speed chases look cool, but you might find it harder to steer your vehicle.
In addition, there are some very limited ways in which you can switch to a first-person perspective. While you're on foot, you can hold the left trigger on your controller and click the right thumbstick. This lets you take a closer look at your surroundings.
Going back to the camera section of the settings menu, you can enable a first-person perspective when your character is looking at their phone. If you look at your phone while you're driving (in GTA 6, never in real life), you'll see your device and the road from a first-person view as well. Perhaps Rockstar will add a proper first-person mode to GTA 6 down the line, as it did with the previous game.

title_en: How to adjust and turn off motion blur in GTA 6 if it makes you feel sick
title_fa: How to adjust and turn off motion blur in GTA 6 if it makes you feel sick
excerpt_en: GTA 6's motion blur effect is thankfully easy to adjust.
excerpt_fa: GTA 6's motion blur effect is thankfully easy to adjust.
content_en:
How to adjust and turn off motion blur in GTA 6 if it makes you feel sick
If the blur makes you feel a little nauseous, there are settings to mitigate it.
If you've been waiting years to play Grand Theft Auto 6, nothing is more disappointing than booting it up and finding it doesn't look quite as good as you'd hoped—or worse, that it makes you feel sick. There are a number of things that could be causing that, but the good news is that one of the most common culprits is extremely easy to fix. Motion blur is a standard feature in most AAA games these days, but there are good reasons some players want to avoid it.
For some people, motion blur just doesn't look good. GTA 6 is the most expensive game ever made, and one reason is its incredibly lifelike graphics. If a layer of motion blur on top of that ruins the illusion, that's enough of a reason to turn it off. Even worse, motion blur commonly contributes to motion sickness, causing dizziness and nausea in some players. Motion blur is nearly ubiquitous in modern games, but fortunately, there are usually settings to tone it down or turn it off completely.
You can tone down GTA 6's motion blur from the pause screen
It's easy to adjust or turn off motion blur in GTA 6. Just pause the game and select Settings from the bottom of the main menu. Next, scroll over to the Display tab by pressing the right shoulder button. About halfway down the page, under the visual effects heading, you'll see a setting called Motion Blur Strength with a slider. By default, it's set to three out of 10, so you can actually tone down the effect without completely turning it off, or even increase it. You can also just set the strength to zero to turn off motion blur completely.
It's worth playing with this setting a little bit to find the level that works for you. Especially at lower frame rates, motion blur can help smooth out camera movements that might otherwise be distractingly jittery, so even leaving it at its lowest level can help. Including a slider instead of a simple toggle is a welcome feature in GTA 6, letting you dial it in to your exact needs.
Since GTA 6 targets 30 fps on consoles, rather than 60 fps, those jarring camera movements may be a bigger deal than they are in other big releases. The best level of motion blur for you will depend more on your TV and personal preference than anything else.

title_en: Here are some photos of Elon Musk, who is 'not MAGA'

excerpt_en: He's not even sure what that means, guys.
excerpt_fa: He's not even sure what that means, guys.
content_en:
Here are some photos of Elon Musk, who is ‘not MAGA’
He's not even sure what that means, guys.
In his first interview since the historic 2026 US midterm elections earlier this month, where he dropped an estimated $446 million on Republicans who overwhelmingly lost their races, Elon Musk denied being affiliated with President Donald Trump's political movement. During an appearance at the the New York Times Dealbook summit, Musk stated, unequivocally, "I'm not MAGA."
Musk joined the event from a hotel in China, where he is one of several US business executives accompanying President Trump on his tour of Asia. "I'm not sure what MAGA means," said the man who is one of the most visible and photographed tech executives to ever live, "but if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican party, then I certainly don't have that." Surely it must be a coincidence that Musk not only owns but seems to regularly wear clothing branded with the phrase.
— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) February 7, 2025
Musk, whose public stature also guarantees that nearly every word he's spoken or tweeted in recent decades immediately becomes a matter of public record, once told an audience of Trump supporters in 2024 "I'm not just MAGA. I'm dark, gothic MAGA." Still, readers should note that he's not MAGA. He doesn't even know what that means!
Pictured above, Musk, who was the de facto head of a federal government agency, gave a Nazi salute, not once, but twice during a speech celebrating Donald Trump's 2024 election win and apparently dresses himself in the dark, appears to have worn MAGA hats in three different colors.
Look, the guy just isn't MAGA. What about this photograph says "blind adherence" to you?

title_en: Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories
title_fa: Former Alibaba exec’s Everful raises $48.5M to connect retailers with Chinese factories
excerpt_en: Everful has raised $48.5 million to expand its factory-direct sourcing platform, helping retailers source products from overseas manufacturers.
excerpt_fa: Everful has raised $48.5 million to expand its factory-direct sourcing platform, helping retailers source products from overseas manufacturers.
content_en:
Everful, a San Francisco- and Singapore-based startup that connects smaller retailers and brands with Chinese factories and manages the process from order to delivery, has raised $48.5 million in Series A funding.
The round was led by Vertex Ventures Southeast Asia & India and January Capital, with participation from existing investors Square Peg and Lightspeed.
Everful is on track to reach $100 million in annualized revenue by the end of the year, about two and a half years after its launch, co-founder Sisi Song said. The company ships over 5 million items a month to customers in more than 60 countries and works with over 30,000 factory partners, she added. Its online wholesale catalog includes more than 20 million products.
Song, a former Alibaba executive, and serial entrepreneur Kevin Han, who sold a previous company to Amazon, co-founded Everful in 2024. The company began as a jewelry wholesale business before evolving into a multi-category, factory-direct sourcing platform.
Retailers and brands often rely on intermediaries, face high minimum order requirements, and experience long sourcing cycles, which tie up capital in inventory before sales trends are clear. Song noticed the growing gap between fast-changing consumer trends and traditional wholesale sourcing models while working as a venture investor at Bessemer Venture Partners, where she mostly focused on cross-border sourcing and meeting numerous startups in the sector. That same gap shaped Everful’s goal to simplify buying directly from factories through an AI-enabled platform.
The B2B sourcing industry is highly competitive. Big Tech giant Alibaba connects international buyers with manufacturers and suppliers, while Faire, a San Francisco-based wholesale tech platform, enables retailers to purchase wholesale inventory directly from brands. According to Everful’s co-founders, its key differentiator is responsibility for the sourcing process, rather than simply facilitating transactions.
“We take care of everything,” Han said. “We handle sourcing, order consolidation, quality control, and logistics. That’s something the marketplaces don’t offer.”
Everful is built for smaller retailers and brands without dedicated sourcing teams, Song said, and it also verifies the factories it works with. While peers also offer services such as quality inspection, logistics, and AI-powered sourcing, Everful aims to integrate these capabilities into a more streamlined purchasing experience, creating an end-to-end process that reduces the work retailers must handle themselves.
Han added that Everful uses AI agents to automate labor-intensive sourcing tasks, including tracking consumer trends, identifying suppliers, coordinating orders across factories, and managing logistics.
Because Everful sources from Chinese factories, ongoing U.S.-China trade tensions and tariffs bear directly on its business. Song said the co-founders have been thinking about geopolitical issues since day one of building the company, and that this has shaped Everful’s strategy from the outset, leveraging her experience at Alibaba and Bessemer Venture Partners.
She mentioned the Trump administration’s suspension of the de minimis exemption, which had allowed eligible shipments valued at $800 or less to enter the U.S. duty-free, as one example of a shift in trade policy.
Song explained such changes could favor a model that combines overseas sourcing with local retail sales. “We’re empowering local retailers and brands,” she said. “Long-term cross-border commerce will be cross-border B2B sourcing plus local selling.”
Everful plans to use the Series A round to expand its presence in the U.S. and Europe, particularly the U.K., France, and Italy, while investing in AI to automate product customization and other sourcing workflows. It also aims to deepen integrations with e-commerce platforms, building on its Shopify integration as it works toward becoming an end-to-end infrastructure platform for global sourcing.
The startup employs about 70 full-time staff globally, including 45 in research and development. It has also established an AI operations team to connect engineering and business functions.

title_en: Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price
title_fa: Anthropic hits Nasdaq exchanges at $111, 33% above IPO price
excerpt_en: Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, representing more than $80 billion in new capital raised.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic's IPO price was set at $83, representing more than $80 billion in new capital raised.
content_en:
Shares of Anthropic are now trading on the Nasdaq exchange, as the company successfully executes its initial public offering. In the early minutes of availability, shares were trading at $111.50, a 33% premium over the $83 IPO price.
Set on Wednesday, the IPO price was already higher than the projected range set by the company, which anticipated a price between $70 and $78 per share. All told, the offering will raise over $81 billion, directed to a combination of employees and the company’s own coffers.
The IPO funding, together with existing fundraising and new private offerings timed to coincide with the company’s public market debut, will leave Anthropic with an expected $220 billion in cash reserves. As one analyst told TechCrunch, “Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had.”
The share price continues to fluctuate, but the opening price would put the company’s market cap over $2 trillion, making it more valuable than Meta, Tesla, or Walmart. Only five companies boast a higher valuation by market cap: Apple, Amazon, Alphabet, Nvidia, and Microsoft.
In a speech before the opening bell, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei emphasized the company’s commitment to safety. “Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing,” Amodei said. “If we can show it’s possible to make the right choices on safety and still build an incredibly successful company, others in our industry will be inspired to do the same. We call this a race to the top.”

title_en: At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development
title_fa: At Nasdaq opening bell, Anthropic CEO recommits to pacing AI development
excerpt_en: In his Nasdaq opening bell speech, Dario Amodei reiterated Anthropic's commitment to pacing AI development, regardless of business or political pressure.
excerpt_fa: In his Nasdaq opening bell speech, Dario Amodei reiterated Anthropic's commitment to pacing AI development, regardless of business or political pressure.
content_en:
As Anthropic made its Wall Street debut on Thursday in the largest IPO in history, CEO Dario Amodei reaffirmed the company’s commitment to developing AI responsibly. In his speech ahead of the Nasdaq opening bell, Amodei vowed that the AI company would not bend to either business or political pressure and would “remain under human control.”
Reading the speech from a printout, the CEO began by talking about Anthropic’s origins as a way to build powerful technology to help humanity — something that he said was inspired by the loss of his father to a disease that became curable just a few years later.
He acknowledged that while human intelligence had made diseases like the plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world, there were still too few scientists with too little time to make progress in other areas of disease. AI, he said, could help with this by working in concert with humans to further medical progress.
It’s telling that Amodei began with a story highlighting AI’s potentially lifesaving applications, since he’s warned repeatedly about the risks of advancing the technology too quickly. In September, Amodei drew headlines when he outlined a plan to pace AI development, which included things like coordinating with other leading companies on safety standards and embedding evaluators from third-party organizations to verify that companies were following their safety commitments.
OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, Google DeepMind chief Demis Hassabis, and xAI owner Elon Musk said they agreed with Amodei’s position, although few concrete commitments have been made.
In this morning’s speech, Amodei again stressed the need to progress AI technology and the safety required in doing so. He referred to the “very real risks” of AI in the hands of bad actors, whether those were individuals or nation-states, and the potential for things like “economic disruption” and “losing control of AI systems.”
Anthropic believes these risks are avoidable, he noted, as long as there are safeguards in place. Amodei said the company would continue to be invested in the work of AI alignment and testing, and developing new ways to understand AI behavior so it could remain under human control.
“There is much work still to be done, and the most difficult safety work lies ahead of us,” he said. “The incredible talent of the company that has enabled us to build the most capable AI systems will need to be directed more so than it has already towards double and triple checking that those AI systems are safe and remain under human control.”
“And to state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control,” Amodei concluded.
His sister, Anthropic co-founder Daniela Amodei, echoed these sentiments in an interview with CNBC on Thursday, noting that while the risks were real, the promise of AI was also “incredible.”
“We were really founded on this idea that it is our job to mitigate those risks, and I think we have to date done an incredible job doing that. We obviously have more work ahead of us, but we are deeply committed to safety,” she added.
The full text of Dario Amodei’s opening speech is below:
Thank you, Daniela. My co-founders and I started Anthropic because we believe that the most powerful technology of our time should be built for the benefit of humankind. Daniela and I lost our father to a disease that just a few years later became curable. I started my career in biology, hoping to help future cures come sooner. In the lab, I saw the vast thicket of complexity that scientists face when they’re trying to understand disease and develop new treatments. So many of the scientific tools that can cut through that thicket — tools for gene editing, tools for gene synthesis, tools for controlling brain cells with light — started as pure ideas. In other words, they came from thinking, from intelligence.
Human intelligence has already made diseases like plague, smallpox, and polio history for most of the world. But progress in other diseases has been too slow for so many patients and their families. Going from a great idea to a treatment can take decades. It took many years from the first discovery of a strange repeating pattern in DNA to the approval of the first treatment for a disease using CRISPR. Nature is full of these patterns, but we’ve had too little intelligence to decipher most of them. Too few scientists with too [little] time. Now we can build that intelligence. Whether it’s protein folding, drug design, cancer genetics, or clinical trial administration, scientists across many areas of biology and medicine are finding Claude can help them do their research in a fraction of the time it would have taken just a couple of years ago. I believe sufficiently powerful AI, working in concert with humans, could compress a century of scientific and medical progress into a decade.
I don’t want to get ahead of myself. At this point, all we have are early results. Experiments and clinical trials will still take time, and although they involve slow and ponderous processes, I believe these processes can be substantially accelerated by AI. We hope that in the future fewer families miss a cure by a few years. Medicine is just a particularly vivid example, but there are many other applications of Claude. Our customers, the world’s most ambitious companies, nonprofits, and individual people, are already applying the intelligence we’ve built to stimulate economic growth, lift people out of poverty, protect democracy and free societies, even make everyday services like the DMV work better. We’re proud to work alongside them, and I’m extremely optimistic about what we can do together in the future.
At the same time, we’ve always been honest that this technology has very real risks. These range from misuse of the technology by individuals or by nation-states to economic disruption to losing control of AI...

title_en: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
title_fa: UK government forced to disclose secret Apple backdoor order
excerpt_en: The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
excerpt_fa: The U.K. tribunal's ruling rejected London's claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
content_en:
The U.K. government has been ordered to confirm that it issued a secret order demanding Apple to provide authorities with encrypted customer information.
The Thursday ruling from the U.K.’s Investigatory Powers Tribunal, an independent court that allows citizens to challenge government surveillance orders, is a rare rebuke for the government, which sought to keep the encryption backdoor order a state secret.
The tribunal’s ruling rejected the Home Office’s claim that disclosing the order would be damaging to national security.
The ruling comes a year after the U.K. government reportedly demanded that Apple build a backdoor to allow U.K. authorities access to customer data anywhere in the world. Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort, arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.
California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.
Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.
Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”
A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.
Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.
A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.
Updated with comment.

Details of the so-called “technical capabilities notice,” which are issued under strict non-disclosure rules, leaked to the media, which drew ire from White House officials and U.S. lawmakers who criticized the effort, arguing that the U.K. order would put Americans’ privacy at risk.
California-based Apple refused the order, and blocked U.K. users from switching on its Advanced Data Protection data-encryption feature for iCloud, rather than comply with the demand. The U.K.’s secret order was later narrowed to allow access to British nationals’ data stored in Apple’s encrypted cloud, and Apple also challenged this second order.
Prior to the ruling, Apple was legally barred from disclosing the order, even after details leaked. When reached for comment, Apple told TechCrunch that it welcomes the decision to make public the fact that the U.K. Home Office issued a technical capability notice.
Apple previously said that it has “never built a backdoor or master key” to any of its products or services and “never will.”
A spokesperson for the U.K. Home Office, which has yet to confirm the existence of a notice, did not respond to a request for comment.
Rights group Liberty International, which brought the legal challenge on behalf of two individuals, said that this is the first known time that the government has been compelled to confirm the existence of a secret technical order.
A final hearing on what specific order details can be released is anticipated next year.

title_en: Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test
title_fa: Anthropic’s IPO puts AI’s circular financing boom to the test
excerpt_en: Anthropic faces enormous compute commitments as it goes public, but its biggest infrastructure partners, including Amazon and Google, could continue profiting from AI even if Anthropic loses its lead.
excerpt_fa: Anthropic faces enormous compute commitments as it goes public, but its biggest infrastructure partners, including Amazon and Google, could continue profiting from AI even if Anthropic loses its lead.
content_en:
Arriving at public markets today, Anthropic’s IPO is poised to raise billions for the company and its investors. But the biggest surprise may be just how much of that money will end up going to supplier-investors.
Amazon and Google, two of Anthropic’s largest infrastructure partners, hold stakes valued around a combined $307.9 billion at the company’s updated IPO price of $83 per share. Amazon, which invested $18 billion into the AI startup, would see its 14.7% stake hit upwards of $159 billion, while Google’s 13.7% stake is valued at nearly $149 billion, according to share ownership figures disclosed in Anthropic’s IPO prospectus.
A handful of other AI infrastructure providers are also positioned to benefit. Nvidia, AMD, Microsoft, Broadcom, Micron, and TSMC have joined Google in committing $26 billion to Anthropic at its IPO price in a private placement.
In total, Google has invested $12.3 billion into Anthropic since 2023, with another promised $30 billion dependent on Anthropic meeting certain performance milestones. And with the exception of TSMC, Anthropic has announced multibillion-dollar strategic partnerships with its other infrastructure supplier investors — including Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Microsoft, and Micron — that would see Anthropic purchasing their products.
This is the circular financing that has made some observers so skeptical of the AI boom. These companies are not just investors; they’re also Anthropic’s biggest suppliers. It might look like Amazon and Google are putting billions into Anthropic, but they get that money right back when Anthropic needs to train a model or serve Claude to users. From afar, it looks like unprecedented revenue growth for cloud companies and unprecedented fundraising from Anthropic — but it’s just the same money passing from one pocket to another.
Today’s IPO marks a critical change in that financing system, the moment it might just become self-sustaining. Those investments appear to have paid off, and are now liquid. Anthropic is still operating at a net loss of tens of billions of dollars each quarter — but it will no longer be suppliers and private investors footing the bill. Now, capital will come from a mix of public-market investors and corporate bonds, neither of which have the conflicts-of-interest that caused concerns before.
And critically, the company’s new bottom line looks pretty good.
Once it debuts, Anthropic is expected to have about $220 billion in cash, cash equivalents, and short-term investments, including proceeds from its IPO and the $26 billion private placement. Anthropic also has the ability to pay for future commitments in stock.
Joey Brookhart, who leads the Tokenomics team at SemiAnalysis, estimates that Anthropic needs roughly $280 billion in cumulative revenue over the next four years to pay for its compute bill, which Brookhart said is “achievable given where they will be next year from a revenue perspective.”
“The ownership stake is very worthwhile, and those companies no longer need any more support from [suppliers],” Brookhart told TechCrunch. “Amazon doesn’t need to prop them up anymore. The revenue is all coming from other customers.”
That doesn’t mean the server bills are going down, though. Anthropic has already committed to spend $900 billion, primarily for compute and infrastructure, according to a regulatory filing. Certain agreements have termination provisions, but Brookhart thinks the company is in a strong position to pay up.
On the other side, Anthropic generated $17 billion in third-quarter 2026 revenue, putting the company on pace for a $68 billion annualized rate for the year. If Anthropic continues to grow at its current trajectory, Brookhart believes it could easily cover the gap needed to fund its compute.
Gil Luria, head of technology research at D.A. Davidson, agreed.
“By the time the IPO is done, Anthropic’s going to have more cash on hand than any company has ever had,” Luria told TechCrunch, noting that the firm raised around $141 billion in capital and will take home around $91.7 billion in net proceeds at $83 per share. “And they’re not burning cash. They’re just going to have a war chest.”
A public listing will make Anthropic a more credible borrower, making it easier to raise money outside of public markets, says Brookhart. That’s despite recent reports that creditors might not see Anthropic as “investment-grade” material.
Luria distinguished between Anthropic’s supplier investments and neoclouds like CoreWeave, which he sees as more purely supported by circular financing. “CoreWeave wouldn’t exist if Nvidia didn’t prop them up, and it probably won’t exist if Nvidia doesn’t bail them out,” Luria said.
Brookhart also pushed back on describing Anthropic’s financing as purely circular, saying it was still “additive to the ecosystem.”
For both analysts, the biggest risk to Anthropic is simply that it will lose the AI race. Right now, the company’s growth is fueled by its status at the frontier of generative AI — but if it’s overtaken by OpenAI, Google DeepMind, or even cheap open-weight models, that could change fast. As Luria put it: “If we’re all using other people’s models, then Anthropic’s not worth a trillion and a half dollars. It’s worth nothing.”
But regardless of who wins the frontier, compute suppliers will likely be just fine. Neither Brookhart nor Luria believe Anthropic’s growth is at risk, despite some arguments that cheaper tokens and more competition will directly affect the AI company’s bottom line.
“For Amazon and Google, the risk isn’t actually that high because in that scenario, we’re using other models,” Luria said. “I’m arguing we’re going to use a lot more AI. I don’t know if it’s all Anthropic’s AI…. That’s still going to come from a data center managed by Amazon, Google, and Microsoft.”

title_en: Nimble enters the item-tracking market with eco-friendly luggage tags and keychains
title_fa: Nimble enters the item-tracking market with eco-friendly luggage tags and keychains
excerpt_en: As Google takes on Apple in the item-tracking market, Nimble is hoping its trackable wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers stand out.
excerpt_fa: As Google takes on Apple in the item-tracking market, Nimble is hoping its trackable wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers stand out.
content_en:
As Google steps up its competition with Apple in the item-tracking market, smaller brands are also looking to carve out a piece of the category. The latest entrant is Nimble, the sustainable accessories brand best known for its charging products.
Founded in 2018 by former Mophie executives, the California-based company announced Thursday that it’s expanding into the category with “Trace,” a seven-product collection of item trackers designed to blend tracking technology into everyday accessories.
Nimble’s new collection arrives as competition in the Bluetooth tracking market continues to heat up. Apple’s AirTag helped popularize the category, while Google recently introduced its first-party tracker, the $29 Pixel Tag, powered by its Find Hub network. Meanwhile, established third-party players, such as Chipolo and Pebblebee, continue to expand their lineups.
Nimble is taking a slightly different approach. Rather than introducing another stand-alone tracker to attach to a set of keys or slip into a bag, the company has integrated tracking technology directly into practical accessories, including wallets, keychains, luggage tags, and passport covers.
The lineup includes seven products, ranging from the $14.95 Trace Tag, which features a replaceable coin-cell battery, to the $49.95 Trace Folio, a passport cover with built-in rechargeable tracking. Other options include the Trace Keyfob ($19.95), Trace Slim Wallet Card ($29.95), Trace Keychain ($29.95), Trace Luggage Tag ($39.95), and Trace Wallet ($39.95).
The entire collection is compatible with both Apple’s Find My and Google’s Find Hub networks.
Ross Howe, co-founder and CEO of Nimble, told us that the company’s approach is designed to differentiate its products from traditional trackers.
“Most locators are built as utility gadgets, not as things you want to own. Few were asking why the locator couldn’t just be the nice object itself. So, for example, we made a wallet findable instead of making a tracker that fits a wallet. We also thought more options should be rechargeable.”
The Trace Luggage Tag and Trace Folio are arguably the most interesting products in the collection. Dedicated luggage tags and passport covers with built-in tracking remain relatively uncommon, giving Nimble an opportunity to stand out in a market. There are only a few alternatives, including Spotminder’s $59 passport cover with Apple Find My support, which is $10 more than Nimble’s option. Knog Scout offers a luggage tag, although I find its design a little too bulky.
Rechargeability is another appealing aspect of Nimble’s new collection. Several models support USB-C or wireless charging, offering an alternative to the disposable batteries found in many traditional trackers. Howe says battery life lasts for “months,” with the Trace Keyfob, for example, rated for approximately six months on a charge.
Sustainability is another major part of Nimble’s pitch. Staying true to its roots, the company has incorporated eco-friendly materials throughout the collection, including recycled plastics and plant-based, vegan aloe leather. The products have also undergone third-party testing for chemicals of concern.
“We’ve spent the last two years going through the chemistry of our products line by line to remove or limit as many harmful ingredients as possible. Trace is the first collection designed specifically to meet these higher standards. We’re not 100% yet, but the independent labs checking our work will help us get there,” Howe said.
The collection is available now through its website and Amazon. All seven products come in five color options: Black, Stone, Tangerine, Plum, and Teal.

title_en: Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere
title_fa: Superhuman pushes its Go assistant everywhere
excerpt_en: Superhuman is making Go its central agent and making it available in Docs and Mail.
excerpt_fa: Superhuman is making Go its central agent and making it available in Docs and Mail.
content_en:
Productivity apps are simultaneously trying to feed more context to their AI tools while also making those AI assistants available in every nook and corner of their products. Superhuman (formerly Grammarly) is going in the same direction with the rollout of features, including a personalized Go assistant, making agents available in Docs, and third-party agent integrations.
While some of the company’s AI features have faced criticism, Superhuman started pushing its Go assistant after its rebranding last year. With the new rollout, it is making Go learn context across different apps and give better personalized suggestions for prompts. Superhuman is revamping its onboarding flow to let users connect their preferred tools and load context about their work upfront.
The assistant works inline with the cursor — just like Grammarly — and also manages other agents. Superhuman is also making the agent proactive, which means it looks for your schedule, keeps an eye on your email, and even drafts responses. The updated Go agent also learns users’ writing styles and responds accordingly in email and Docs.
The productivity company is adding 20 new connected agents, including DeepL, Legora, Amplitude, Databricks, and Blackboard, through its Go SDK.
The company is also thinking about adding AI to different products, including Docs and Superhuman Mail. In Docs, all Go agents work natively, and you can set them off to work on different tasks in the background. Users can also set routines to trigger workflows based on events.
Until now, Mail has used AI as its central tool, which is being replaced by Go. Users can also do enterprise search by using data from the company knowledge base and connected tools. Go also uses this context to form drafts and organize the inbox across Google and Outlook accounts.
Superhuman acquired notetaker Fathom in September to add more context to its suite. The company is now rolling out live collaborative notetaking, which would be shared across the team. Plus, Go can now make decisions post-meeting, like forming an initial draft of a proposal.
The company’s CEO, Shishir Mehrotra, said that Go has had good momentum with over 1 million active users. There are a host of agents now that are vying for users’ attention on both the personal and professional front. Mehrotra thinks that while Go is more work-focused, it can help with personal emails and schedules.
“One of the reasons why these assistants have been popular is that they treat you as a whole person and recognize that we need to cover both extremes. Go is definitely more work-focused than some of the tools coming out of the pure consumer ecosystem. It doesn’t mean we draw the boundary at helping you with your personal tasks or helping you with your calendar or all of your email,” he told TechCrunch over a call.
While Go might not directly compete with the likes of Instinct, Muse, and Fo, Superhuman wants users to choose its assistant over something like OpenAI’s Dots or Claude Duet.

title_en: DOJ accuses Russian national of spying on and harassing Palantir employees
title_fa: DOJ accuses Russian national of spying on and harassing Palantir employees
excerpt_en: The DOJ says the Russian national was ordered to spy on Palantir over Ukraine's use of its software for wartime purposes.
excerpt_fa: The DOJ says the Russian national was ordered to spy on Palantir over Ukraine's use of its software for wartime purposes.
content_en:
DOJ accuses Russian national of spying on and harassing Palantir employees
He allegedly took photos of their work laptops and even once followed a female employee for 30 miles.
A Russian national has been indicted for spying on and harassing the employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company, according to the Department of Justice. While the agency's announcement didn't name the specific company, Bloomberg reports that it was Palantir, and that the Russian national was told to do so over Ukraine's use of the company's software for wartime purposes.
Igor D'iu was reportedly recruited by the Russian government through Telegram, where he also received orders on what to do, the DOJ says. He traveled from Istanbul, Turkey to Mexico City, from where he illegally crossed the border to the US in June 2026. On US soil, he was made to purchase laptops, phones, remote access software and wireless networking equipment. He was told that that the company he was monitoring "was providing weapons to fight against Russia in Ukraine."
The Russian officials he was in contact with told him to visit a coffee shop near Palantir's Palo Alto office and take photos of its employees' laptop screens. They also made him switch on his laptop at designated areas near the company's offices, so they could remotely access and collect information from the devices of employees in the vicinity.
His assignment included the surveillance of Palantir employees and their homes, as well. In September, he allegedly followed a female employee in a car for more than 30 miles. D'iu's home was searched on October 8, where authorities found two Russian passports and $18,035 in cash. Authorities had also intercepted packages for him shipped from overseas, containing a fake California ID card and an authentic US passport altered with his photograph.
Palantir, a tech company, is controversial for providing governments, law enforcement and the military products they can then use for mass surveillance. Wired previously reported that ICE used a database built by the company to compile dossiers on people accused of observing and protesting its activities. According to Bloomberg, the US uses Palantir's technology to offer targeting support to Ukraine. In addition, Ukrainian forces in Kyiv use its products for various purposes, including the removal of unexploded Russian mines in the country.
D'iu has been charged with "one count of conspiracy to act as an agent of a foreign government, one count of acting as an agent of a foreign government without notice to the Attorney General, one count of interstate stalking and one count of fraud in connection with identification documents." He is scheduled to appear in federal court on November 24.

title_en: Elon Musk accuses Ukraine of being 'untruthful' about Starshield disruptions
title_fa: Elon Musk accuses Ukraine of being 'untruthful' about Starshield disruptions
excerpt_en: Elon Musk has accused Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being 'untruthful' about Starshield disruptions.
excerpt_fa: Elon Musk has accused Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being 'untruthful' about Starshield disruptions.
content_en:
Elon Musk accuses Ukraine of being 'untruthful' about Starshield disruptions
He said that Ukraine is trying to use SpaceX’s consumer Starlink service for military purposes.
Elon Musk has accused Ukraine president Volodymyr Zelenskyy of being "untruthful" about Starshield disruptions hampering the nation's ability to defend and fight back against Russia. The SpaceX CEO told The New York Times' DealBook Summit that Ukraine is actually trying to use the company's consumer Starlink service, not Starshield, for military purposes.
"From the beginning, I've said that Starlink is a civilian system," Musk told interviewer Andrew Ross Sorkin. "It is not meant to be used for offensive drone strikes that kill people. If you want to do that, you need to use Starshield, which is a separate system that is controlled by the US government. But do not ask me as a private individual to make kill decisions."
Musk's comments come amid a lengthy disruption to Starshield in Ukraine. Last month, Zelenskyy posted on X that speed limits on Starshield were imposed along the war's entire front line and in Russian territory, saying any terminal moving faster than 161 km/h (100 mph) would lose its connection to the satellite network. "Unfortunately, this is helping the Russians kill more Ukrainians and carry out more accurate strikes against Ukraine," Zelenskyy said at the time. "We are trying to establish all the circumstances with the American side."

title_en: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
title_fa: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explains why he asked 60K employees to quit
excerpt_en: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit, rather than reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. The short answer is AI, but not in the way you might expect.
excerpt_fa: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit, rather than reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. The short answer is AI, but not in the way you might expect.
content_en:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff.
Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He’s not saying he’s replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He’s saying he’s reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI.
The buyout was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit.
“Let’s take software engineering. We went from, ‘Well, we don’t buy that AI can ever do software.’ To suddenly, ‘Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?’ To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point,” he explained.
For some people, “that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?” he added, “but, I mean, it has to be done.”
He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. “They build a software factory that builds the product. They don’t build the product.”
He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. “That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs.”
But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn’t grow up as an AI-first company. “So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?” he said. “It’s going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, ‘Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.’”
When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, “We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don’t have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution.”
He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. “All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity.”
In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere.

title_en: Elon Musk says: ‘I’m not MAGA’
title_fa: Elon Musk says: ‘I’m not MAGA’
excerpt_en: During his appearance Wednesday at The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk said that he wasn't sure what the term "MAGA" meant and also commented that he felt "pretty foolish" for having spent so much money during the U.S. midterms.
excerpt_fa: During his appearance Wednesday at The New York Times' DealBook Summit, Elon Musk said that he wasn't sure what the term "MAGA" meant and also commented that he felt "pretty foolish" for having spent so much money during the U.S. midterms.
content_en:
Elon Musk, who spent $277 million to get Donald Trump reelected president in 2024 and who, during that campaign, declared himself “dark MAGA” and who, after the election, was subsequently photographed sporting a cartoonishly large MAGA hat while visiting the Oval Office, has some news for Americans: None of that necessarily makes him MAGA.
“I’m not MAGA,” Musk declared Wednesday during a conversation with Andrew Ross Sorkin at The New York Times DealBook Summit. Musk joined the conversation via video call, as he is currently in China, joining President Trump for the APEC summit.
“Well, at least I’m not like … I’m not sure what MAGA means,” he backtracked. “If that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”
The comments were made amidst a broader question about how Musk felt in the wake of this year’s midterms, during which a “blue wave” led to Democratic victories throughout the country. Musk, notably, spent a gargantuan amount of money (reportedly some $445 million) to support Republican candidates. Musk admitted Wednesday that such vast political spending might not have been a good use of his money.
“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seen much for it,” he said. “Or maybe it would have been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that, you know, American elections are not just about money.”
During his conversation with Sorkin, Musk also seemed to lean away from his viral edgelord persona and claimed that he held no extreme views. He said: “I don’t think I have like, you know, any kind of extreme political views.”
Sorkin pushed Musk on this a little, noting that some people found his views on immigration extreme, to which Musk said: “Like what?” Mild laughter spread throughout the audience.
Ironically, the last time Musk spoke at DealBook, in 2023, he was in the middle of a very public battle with his social media site X’s advertisers. Critics had accused Musk of platforming a typhoon of hateful content on his site, and advertisers were threatening to walk over it. In response, Musk famously told Sorkin that he hoped those advertisers would “go f—” themselves.
Now Musk has an entirely new set of concerns. Democratic lawmakers in various committees have signaled that they may investigate Musk and his business activities as they probe potential corruption throughout the Trump administration.
Specifically, officials have said they’re interested in scrutinizing Musk’s role in DOGE, the “government efficiency” initiative that Musk launched inside the White House at the start of Trump’s new term, as well as Starlink’s activities in Ukraine, where the company has been accused of throttling the military’s access to its internet service.
Sorkin broached some of the potential concerns for the Tesla CEO: “You hear people like the chairman of the oversight committee saying, ‘Lawyer up,’ and you hear the president saying, ‘If I have to give him a pardon’ — meaning you — ‘I’ll give him a pardon.’”
Musk replied: “I don’t think I need a pardon by the way, because I haven’t committed any crimes.”
Musk then made one of those controversial statements he’s known for, appearing to compare an incoming Texas official to Lavrentiy Beria, the top head of the Soviet secret police under Josef Stalin.
“The incoming Texas, you know, House Majority Leader, said that I should go to prison,” Musk said. “I’m like, the guy’s trying to, you know channel Beria from, like, Stalin, where it’s, you know, show me the man, I’ll show you the crime type of thing.”
It’s not clear who (or what) Musk was talking about. Texas doesn’t have a House Majority Leader. However, he may have been referencing Gene Wu, who is the incoming chair of the Texas House Democratic caucus and who has suggested that Musk be investigated for potential criminal activity.
“Hopefully, in this country, you still need to do an actual crime before you go to prison,” Musk added.

title_en: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’
title_fa: Amidst fears of AI cyberattacks, Satya Nadella says lots of critical infrastructure is ‘unpatchable’
excerpt_en: The Microsoft CEO downplayed the recent Outlook outage while noting that AI was causing both opportunities and new challenges for securing much of the connected world.
excerpt_fa: The Microsoft CEO downplayed the recent Outlook outage while noting that AI was causing both opportunities and new challenges for securing much of the connected world.
content_en:
During his appearance at The New York Times’ DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella lamented the fact that a lot of America’s software systems — including those governing everyday hardware and transportation systems — suffer from unfixable software vulnerabilities that, in the age of AI-aided cyberattacks, are just waiting to be exploited.
“Remember, there is a lot of stuff in our critical infrastructure that’s unpatchable,” Nadella said. “I mean, think about all the firmware and the chillers [a cooling device often used in data centers] and the HVAC systems everywhere else. So all of that, by the way, they’re on the internet.”
In other words: The smartification of the economy, in which much of the world’s “dumb” devices were hooked up to the internet, is now causing tremendous headaches.
The conversation took place against the backdrop of a wave of recent large-scale outages — including one involving Microsoft Outlook. Others have involved the NSA, the FFA, and Apple. Concerns have swirled that these outages are the result of cyberattacks, although officials have denied those claims. Still, the reality of AI-aided cyberattacks is spurring companies to find new strategies for vulnerability discovery and remediation.
Nadella touched briefly on the recent Outlook situation, noting that the global inconvenience was the result of a “latent bug” that led to a “perfect storm.”
“We put out an incident response, and we’re going to obviously take all of the learnings, both upstream architectural, as well as operational, and fix that,” he added.
“Somebody was telling me about sort of even the transportation systems and the amount of stuff that’s discoverable but with unpatchable firmware,” Nadella also added on the topic of vulnerable systems. “So we’ll have to really modernize for sure … and then we will have to assess what the threat vector looks like, what our own ability to both detect and then defend in real time looks like.”
Nadella made a broader point as well, which is that the process of patching software vulnerabilities has escalated to match the speed of potential exploitation, but that this has caused more problems.
“We now have a very powerful tool that finds vulnerabilities,” he said. However, companies used to have more time to test those patches, understand a situation, and deploy them, he said. At the same time, AI has made sophisticated cyberattacks much easier to enact.
“The patch [now] needs to go instantly from being available to being patched in production, because it’s being exploited in the wild, right? So that’s going to create instability.”

title_en: Elon Musk says ousting Jensen Huang is like ‘kicking Michael Jordan off your team’
title_fa: Elon Musk says ousting Jensen Huang is like ‘kicking Michael Jordan off your team’
excerpt_en: “I don’t think [Huang is] disloyal to the United States," Musk said.
excerpt_fa: “I don’t think [Huang is] disloyal to the United States," Musk said.
content_en:
Elon Musk has already been vocal about his disapproval of the Nvidia board’s decision to oust its founder and CEO Jensen Huang after a series of extramarital affairs were made public, including one with an alleged Chinese spy who is suspected of feeding sensitive information back to Beijing. At The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday, Musk elaborated on his thoughts about Nvidia’s leadership change.
“Jensen is an old friend of mine,” Musk said. “I would call Jensen, you know, Michael Jordan at his peak level, in terms of what he means to a team.”
On X, the social media platform he owns, Musk even said he would hire Huang.
“He’s one of the most talented entrepreneur-CEOs in history,” Musk said when asked about his X post. “Who wouldn’t want to hire Jensen?”
Musk also signed a petition, alongside over 200,000 other people, urging Nvidia to reinstate its former CEO. Nvidia’s board, however, confirmed it is not planning to bring Huang back.
“[It] doesn’t seem like a smart decision to me…” Musk said of that decision. “There’s no one that can really replace Jensen.”
Huang “has long-term relationships that have been built up over decades,” Musk added. “He understands technology incredibly well. His team loves him… and many of them are there because of him, and have higher offers to go elsewhere, and have turned them down because of personal loyalty to Jensen.”
Anduril CEO Palmer Luckey also said that he thinks Nvidia is making the wrong decision by not reinstating Huang.
“China wants Jensen out, so I want him in,” Luckey said earlier in the day at the DealBook event. “They’re thrilled to have Jensen out… There’s a reason it’s knocking a trillion dollars off Nvidia’s market cap. They know it makes America weaker to knock him out.”
Musk also did not express concern over what Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy could mean for U.S. national security.
“I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States,” Musk said. “I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders.”
Other peers in the industry, like Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, reaffirmed their faith in Nvidia to move forward without its founder and CEO of 33 years at the helm.
“It’s the Nvidia board’s decision, but I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella said at DealBook. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”

“I don’t think he’s disloyal to the United States,” Musk said. “I think it’s like kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you’re on a winning streak, and it just doesn’t seem like a good thing for shareholders.”
Other peers in the industry, like Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, reaffirmed their faith in Nvidia to move forward without its founder and CEO of 33 years at the helm.
“It’s the Nvidia board’s decision, but I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella said at DealBook. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO of Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”

title_en: Waymo pauses service in San Francisco after robotaxis get stuck on flooded streets
title_fa: Waymo pauses service in San Francisco after robotaxis get stuck on flooded streets
excerpt_en: Waymo temporarily paused service in San Francisco after several robotaxis caused traffic jams as they were unable to navigate flooded streets during a storm.
excerpt_fa: Waymo temporarily paused service in San Francisco after several robotaxis caused traffic jams as they were unable to navigate flooded streets during a storm.
content_en:
Waymo pauses service in San Francisco after robotaxis get stuck on flooded streets
This isn’t the first time the company’s robotaxis have caused chaos in the city.
Waymo has temporarily paused its robotaxi service in San Francisco due to issues dealing with flooding on some streets, according to an X post from District 5 Supervisor Bilal Mahmood and a message in the Waymo app. The interruption in service follows several incidents of Waymos blocking intersections because they're seemingly unable (or unwilling) to drive through water.
Riders who want to get picked up are now greeted with a message in the app that says "we're paused for now due to weather" and that service will resume "when road conditions improve and the forecast looks clear." San Francisco is currently dealing with heavy rain and flooding as the region heads into what forecasters expect could be a record El Niño winter.
Ahead of the pause, videos posted on X showed a Waymo stopped in the middle of a flooded crosswalk, forcing cars to drive around it. Another Waymo idled in the middle of a road and instructed its rider to stay inside.
WATCH: Waymo robotaxi gets STUCK in a flooded San Francisco intersection as an atmospheric river swamps the Bay Area
> Waymo paused its Bay Area robotaxi service around 11 AM local time, saying it will return when roads improve
> Downtown SF got about 2.11 inches of rain before... pic.twitter.com/txR939p4Qf— James Reichert (@_jamesreichert) November 18, 2026
Engadget has asked Waymo to comment on the stalled robotaxis and the issues it's facing with San Francisco's current weather. We'll update this article if we hear back.
Waymo previously paused service in San Francisco in December 2025, when a power outage led to similar instances of robotaxis blocking city streets. The company has also dealt with flooding in the past. In May, Waymo recalled nearly 4,000 vehicles and paused its service after a robotaxi drove into a flooded road in San Antonio. The company issued a software update to address the issue, but later had to pause service in Atlanta when a Waymo drove into a flooded street again.
The fact that the company is dealing with these issues in San Francisco suggests solving this problem might be more complicated than it appears. The pause only affects the city, but it comes just a day after the California DMV restricted Waymo from the state's freeways, prompting the company to pull its robotaxis off freeways in all of its markets.

title_en: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
title_fa: The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
excerpt_en: New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable...
excerpt_fa: New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable...
content_en:
New York, Los Angeles, and Chicago schools are considering Google alternatives after the company said it will disable Search for schools that opt out of its AI features, according to The New York Times. Starting next year, schools will not have the option to disable Gemini-powered features without also disabling Search. Chris Phillips, Google’s vice president of education, told the Times that, “Search and AI are deeply integrated,” and that schools that turn off Google’s AI features “will not have access to Search.”
The nation’s largest school districts consider ditching Google Search
Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.
Google is trying to force Gemini on schools, and they’re not thrilled.
Many elected officials, including New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and Senator Bernie Sanders, responded harshly, calling Google’s behavior “extortion.” Mamdani had recently announced a policy that barred 2-K-8 students from using AI in the classroom. In a statement to the Times, New York City schools chancellor Kamar H. Samuels said, “If Google doesn’t reconsider their position, we will explore other search options.” Chicago’s public schools have also reportedly told Google that if it can’t provide a version of Search without AI, “the district will look to other search solutions.”
In a statement to The Verge, Google spokesperson Laura Breen said, “We hear parents and teachers’ concerns about students using AI to shortcut learning, and we share the same goal: help students learn. To improve Search for the classroom, we’re starting to pilot Guided Learning capabilities in Search this month to walk students step-by-step through a range of complex problems, instead of just giving quick answers. Next year, we’re also updating our approach to controls for schools to address feedback we’ve heard from educators, so Gemini app, Gemini Notebook and Search will be off by default until schools decide which services to enable. We are actively building these experiences in partnership with educators, listening closely to ensure our products support students and teachers.”
Educators are wary of AI’s effect on students’ critical thinking skills, and some studies have shown that students who use AI generally perform worse on tests. There are also concerns about the mental health effects on children who develop relationships with chatbots at a young age. But Google is deeply embedded in classrooms across the US, which rely on Google Classroom, Chromebooks, and other services, and going fully Google-free might prove difficult.

title_en: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remains confident in Nvidia after Huang’s exit
title_fa: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella remains confident in Nvidia after Huang’s exit
excerpt_en: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella expressed confidence in Jensen Huang's successor Colette Kress, who is serving as Nvidia's interim CEO.
excerpt_fa: Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella expressed confidence in Jensen Huang's successor Colette Kress, who is serving as Nvidia's interim CEO.
content_en:
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella weighed in on former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s unexpected departure amid a series of shocking controversies.
“It’s all sort of pretty tragic in the sense of, you know, Jensen is somebody I’ve known for a long time. I’ve admired what he’s done, and at this point, I kind of want to give him space to figure this out,” Nadella said onstage at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Wednesday.
Huang stepped down last week from his CEO role, which he has held for 33 years. Huang’s leadership has been central to Nvidia’s ascent to one of the world’s most valuable companies, but his judgment was questioned after it was reported that he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials believe is a Chinese spy feeding information back to Beijing. It was also revealed that Huang was having affairs with two Nvidia employees, including one who was a direct report.
While the world waits to see what the long-term economic impacts of Huang’s departure might be, Nadella says he still has confidence in Nvidia, which is a close partner of Microsoft.
“I’ll just say this one thing,” Nadella added. “Colette [Kress, interim CEO at Nvidia] worked at Microsoft for a long time. I’ve known her for a long time. She’s a tremendous person… I’m in touch with the same set of people I was in touch with before [Huang left], so I have a lot of confidence in the Nvidia team and their ability to continue to do the good work.”
Microsoft is not unlike Nvidia in that its founder Bill Gates inhabited a larger-than-life persona as CEO.
“Founders are unbelievable in the sense that they create something from nothing, so that is pretty magical… They’re singular, but they’re not gods, right?” Nadella said. “I used to say to Bill [Gates]… Founders also die, and so at some point, a company, if it needs to succeed, it has to have someone take over.”
